will have haploid individuals carrying the alleles of type A and B. In the Wright-Fisher
model we will have diploid individuals carrying a pair of alleles of types A and B in one
autosomal locus. Although these two models diﬀer in structure and complexity, it is still
possible to provide a common description of the underlying process of selection and drift.
We start by considering a population of N alleles. To allow for a common treatment of
both models we will assume that N is an even number. At any point in time, NA and
NB are the number of alleles of type A and B in the population, respectively, and at
each time point NA +NB = N holds. We will say that NA and NB are the frequencies of
alleles A and B, respectively. Throughout the whole manuscript, we assume that these
frequencies can be measured exactly (no sampling errors).
We will follow the fate of the number of alleles of type B whose dynamics will be
described as a Markov chain in discrete time with two absorbing states in NB = 0 and

matches.excerpt:
Using a Markov Chain Monte Carlo optimization algorithm and a computer sim-
ulation, I ﬁnd the passenger ordering which minimizes the time required to board
the passengers onto an airplane. The model that I employ assumes that the time
that a passenger requires to load his or her luggage is the dominant contribution
to the time needed to completely ﬁll the aircraft. The optimal boarding strategy
may reduce the time required to board and airplane by over a factor of four and
possibly more depending upon the dimensions of the aircraft. In addition, knowl-
edge of the optimal boarding procedure can inform decisions regarding changes to
methods that are employed by a particular carrier. I explore some of the salient
features of the optimal boarding method and discuss practical modiﬁcations to the
optimal. Finally, I mention some of the beneﬁts that could come from implementing
an improved passenger boarding scheme.

matches.doc_title: Gaussian Process Kernels for Pattern Discovery and Extrapolation
matches.excerpt:
We have only begun to explore what could be done
with such pattern discovery methods. In future work,
one could integrate away a spectral density, using re-
cently developed eﬃcient Markov chain Monte Carlo
for GP hyperparameters (Murray & Adams, 2010).
Moreover, recent Toeplitz methods (Saatchi, 2011)
could be applied to the SM kernel for signiﬁcant
speedup in inference and predictions.

[12] R. Salakhutdinov and A. Mnih. Bayesian probabilistic matrix
factorization using Markov chain Monte Carlo. In Interna-
tional Conference on Machine learning, 2008.

sampled from the gametes from the previous generation, in which the frequency of the
alleles A and B have been determined through the evolutionary dynamics. The number
NB of alleles of type B in a ﬁnite adult population thus changes randomly from one
generation to the next as a result of selection and drift (Methods). Also here the number
of alleles NB is described as a Markov chain with two absorbing states in 0 and N,
corresponding to the ﬁxation of allele A and B, respectively.
This model is numerically more challenging than the Moran model. In particular, the
time scale to ﬁxation is shorter than for the Moran model because here the generations
are non-overlapping. Here, thus, each trajectory has a duration of T = 100 generations.
As for the Moran model, we have generated 100 independent time-series for each of the
four types (Fig.

closer to the true value.

The models that we consider have two types of alleles, A and B. In the Moran model we
will have haploid individuals carrying the alleles of type A and B. In the Wright-Fisher
model we will have diploid individuals carrying a pair of alleles of types A and B in one
autosomal locus. Although these two models diﬀer in structure and complexity, it is still
possible to provide a common description of the underlying process of selection and drift.
We start by considering a population of N alleles. To allow for a common treatment of
both models we will assume that N is an even number. At any point in time, NA and
NB are the number of alleles of type A and B in the population, respectively, and at
each time point NA +NB = N holds. We will say that NA and NB are the frequencies of
alleles A and B, respectively. Throughout the whole manuscript, we assume that these
frequencies can be measured exactly (no sampling errors).
We will follow the fate of the number of alleles of type B whose dynamics will be
described as a Markov chain in discrete time with two absorbing states in NB = 0 and
NB = N. These two absorbing states correspond to the ﬁxation of allele A and B,
respectively.

I now have enough to answer completely. The corpus-wide keyword search covered all 100 documents, and I've verified the two documents that genuinely build a *model* on a Markov chain versus the many that merely mention Markov-chain *Monte Carlo* as a sampling technique.

---

## "Markov chain model" — what the corpus actually contains

Searching all 100 PDFs, "Markov chain" appears in **8 documents**, but in two distinct senses. Only two documents actually use a Markov chain *as a model of a system*; the rest cite **Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC)**, which is a sampling algorithm, not a model. Here is the complete picture.

### Documents that genuinely use a Markov chain as a model

**1. Population-genetics allele dynamics — `1606.06090.pdf`** (the clearest "Markov chain model" in the corpus)

This paper models the number of alleles of a given type in a finite population as a **discrete-time Markov chain with two absorbing states**, corresponding to fixation of either allele.
- **Page 3** — The Moran model: "We will follow the fate of the number of alleles of type B whose dynamics will be described as a Markov chain in discrete time with two absorbing states in N_B = 0 and N_B = N."
- **Page 5** — The model's mathematics rest explicitly on the Markov property: the relationship between conditioned and non-conditioned transition probabilities is derived "by exploiting the Markov property of the chains."
- **Page 8** — The Wright-Fisher variant: "the number of alleles N_B is described as a Markov chain with two absorbing states in 0 and N," and the analysis proceeds "using the transition probabilities of this model."

**2. Market making as a Markov decision process — `2607.08291.pdf`** ("Robustness in Sequential Decision Making under Evolving Uncertainty…")

This paper formulates its problem as an MDP — a controlled Markov chain (states + actions + transition dynamics).
- **Page 5** — "We formulate market making as a finite-horizon sequential decision problem. We begin with a baseline market-making model that serves as the reference **Markov decision process**. The model describes the economic environment, the state and action spaces."
- **Page 3** — It builds on the **robust MDP** framework, where "transition dynamics [are allowed] to vary within an uncertainty set."
- (Its reference list on pages 32/34 also cites classic robust-MDP / "Markov chains" literature — those are citations, not the paper's own model.)

### Documents where "Markov chain" means MCMC (a sampling method, not a model)

For completeness — these matched the query but do **not** build a Markov-chain model; they use MCMC to sample posteriors or integrate out parameters:

- **`0802.0733.pdf`, p.1** — uses a "Markov Chain Monte Carlo optimization algorithm" to find an optimal airplane-boarding order.
- **`1302.4245.pdf`, pp.3, 4, 9** (Gaussian Process kernels) — MCMC to integrate out GP hyperparameters.
- **`2607.06755.pdf`, p.12** (galaxy gravity/anisotropy) — the `emcee` affine-invariant MCMC ensemble sampler.
- **`2607.06844.pdf`, p.6** (ultra-fast outflows) — parameter uncertainties "estimated via Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) sampling."
- **`1501.05624.pdf`, p.10** — a *reference* to Bayesian probabilistic matrix factorization using MCMC.
- **`0707.4042.pdf`, p.15** — a *reference* to Keilson's book *Markov Chain Models—Rarity and Exponentiality*.

### Bottom line

If "Markov chain model" means a system modeled *as* a Markov chain, the corpus has two answers:
- **`1606.06090.pdf` (pp. 3, 5, 8)** — allele-frequency evolution as a discrete-time Markov chain with absorbing (fixation) states; the strongest match.
- **`2607.08291.pdf` (pp. 3, 5)** — market making as a (robust) Markov decision process.

All other matches are the **MCMC** sampling algorithm and do not describe a Markov-chain model.

One caveat: semantic search was unavailable on this server (fastembed not installed), so this ran as keyword search — it reliably finds the literal phrase "Markov chain" but could miss a paper that models a Markov process without using that exact wording.
